# Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Established 

Bain News Service, photographer. Italians around suspended bank. NYC. [between 1907 and 1914]. Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), an independent agency of the federal government, was created by the Banking Act of 1933 in response to the thousands of bank failures that occurred in the 1920s and early 1930s. According to the FDIC, their mission is to "maintain stability and public confidence in the nation's financial system by insuring deposits, examining and supervising commercial and savings banks, working to make large and complex financial institutions resolvable, and managing receiverships." In this way, the agency prevents “run-on-the-bank” scenarios or “bank panics,” which occur when a group of concerned customers rush to withdraw money from the bank. This type of panic resulted in the failure of many banks during the Great Depression and contributed to the loss of the Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) in March 2023.

The FDIC is funded by premiums that banks and savings associations pay for deposit insurance coverage. The standard insurance amount is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category and is automatic. The insurance is backed by the full faith and insurance of the U.S. government. FDIC insured banks have the following assets covered by this insurance: checking accounts, savings accounts (both statement and passbook), Money Market Deposit Accounts (MMDAs), and Certificates of Deposit (CDs). This deposit insurance does not insure assets from institutions not insured by the FDIC as well as the following types of investments: cryptocurrency, mutual funds, stocks, bonds, annuities, and any investment that is not a deposit.

The FDIC has a supervisory program where it monitors the safety and soundness of its supervised institutions to anticipate and avoid problems. The agency employs a resolution process for failing banks, and a receivership process for failed banks. When a bank closes, the FDIC is typically appointed as the receiver and is responsible for resolving the failed institution. The FDIC played a primary role in stabilizing the banking system during various periods of turmoil in U.S. history, including during the Great Depression (1930s) when there was widespread bank failures, the Savings and Loan Crisis (1980s–early 1990s) when there was a collapse of many of these institutions due to risky lending practices and interest rate volatility, and the Financial Crisis (2007–2008) caused by a variety of factors including: subprime mortgage lending, excessive risk taking, lax regulation, a housing bubble, the collapse of major financial institutions, a credit freeze, and a severe economic recession. In response to the Financial Crisis, the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act was passed on July 21, 2010. Despite these enhanced legislative initiatives, on March 10, 2023, SVB failed due to mismanagement, its investments losing value while its depositors began withdrawing large amounts of assets. 1 After the collapse of SVB, Signature Bank failed and other institutions faltered. Regulatory agencies came under scrutiny for not anticipating issues earlier concerning the soundness of SVB.

Part of the FDIC's charter is to protect consumers rights and promote community investment initiatives. The FDIC Money Smart financial education program can help people of all ages enhance their financial skills and create positive banking relationships. In addition, the agency provides detailed economic and financial data for a variety of users.

## Print Resources 

The following titles link to fuller bibliographic information in the Library of Congress Online Catalog. Links to digital content are provided when available.

- Bailout: An Insider's Account of Bank Failures and Rescues by Irvine H. Sprague 

 Call Number: HG2491 .S67 2000 

 Published/Created: 2000-06-01 

 The author was intermittent FDIC chairman from the early 1970s to the mid-1980s, a time when banks were dealing with high interest rates, a downturn in the commercial real estate market, fluctuating energy prices, and a debt crisis with less developed countries. The book discusses how the FDIC handled four bank failures, in contrast to the S&L Home Loan Bank Board, these institutions were closed and sold at no cost to the taxpayers. 
- Bull by the Horns by Sheila Bair 

 Call Number: HG2491 .B23 2012 

 Published/Created: 2012-09-25 

 Sheila Bair was appointed by President George W. Bush as the chairman of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) in 2006. Bair warned of the risks of subprime-mortgage-backed bonds and became one of the lead players in the government’s response to the 2008-2009 financial crisis. 
- Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and National Credit Union Administration by Joe M. Wallace (Editor); Keith R. Barnes (Editor) 

 Call Number: HG1662.U5 F432 2012 

 Published/Created: 2012-09-01 

 The FDIC was established as an independent government corporation under the authority of the Banking Act of 1933. The agency is funded through insurance assessments collected from its member depository institutions and held in what is now known as the Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF). The proceeds in the DIF are used to pay depositors if member institutions fail. This book provides an overview of the FDIC, recent status of DIF, and efforts to reduce the loss exposure and total risk to the fund. The book also addresses the credit union system and the National Credit Union Administration. 
- Inside the FDIC by John F. Bovenzi 

 Call Number: HG1662 .U5 

 Published/Created: 2015-01-20 

 The text tells the real stories behind bank failures and financial crises to provide a direct account of the FDIC and other bank regulators. The author served in senior level positions within the FDIC for over twenty years, including a decade as the Deputy to the Chairman and Chief Operating Officer. This book describes what he witnessed as the person in charge of day-to-day operations, as a nearly invisible agency grew to become a major, highly independent force impacting US financial markets. 
- Insolvency Issues and the FDIC by Philip B. Williamson (Editor) 

 Call Number: HG1662.U5 I565 2010 

 Published/Created: 2010-08-01 

 This book discusses actions taken by the FDIC in support of financial and housing markets during the Financial Crisis, which include restoration of the Deposit Insurance Fund, the development of the Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program, efforts to reduce foreclosures, and established of the proposed Public-Private Investment Fund. The Depositor Protection Act of 2009 has also been introduced to increase the effectiveness of the FDIC's efforts to respond to recent market weaknesses. A brief analysis of some important differences between the FDIC's conservatorship/receivership authority and that of the Bankruptcy Code is given. 

## Library of Congress Digital Resources 

The following resources created and digitized by the Library of Congress can be used to find out more about the FDIC as well as important events in U.S. financial history.

- 1933 Bank Holiday, This Month in Business History by Science, Technology & Business Division 

 Published/Created: 2023 

 The U.S. was in the grip the Great Depression that began in 1929. Belief in Wall Street and the country's banking system was shaken. Hundreds of banks failed and the banking system was under strain. Franklin D. Roosevelt was inaugurated on March 4, 1933 and less than 48 hours into his presidency, he issued Proclamation 2039 which suspended all banking activity. 
- Business Booms, Busts, & Bubbles: A Resource Guide on Economic Manias & Crashes by Science, Technology and Business Division 

 Published/Created: 2022 

 This research guide brings together background and resources on a few economic bubbles with a lasting impact like the South Sea Bubble, Tulip Mania, dot-com bubbles, and stock market crashes, as well as historical business cycles in general. 
- Chronicling America, Historic American Newspapers 

 Historic American newspapers selected covering and contributed by state partners in the National Digital Newspaper Program, covering the period of 1770-1963. You can search for news prior to and including1963 by searching keywords such as the "FDIC," and the "Banking Act of 1933." 
- Congressional Record 

 This is the source for the Congressional Record back to 1899 and is where to find what was said on the House and Senate floor. For instance, you can search for the "Glass-Steagall Act" and the "Consumer Financial Protection Act." 
- National Recovery Administration (NRA) and the New Deal: A Resource Guide by Science, Technology and Business Division 

 Published/Created: 2020 

 This guide contains resources related to period and may be of interest. There is an inventory of some material produced by the National Recovery Act as well as resources related to many of the New Deal activities. 
- Wall Street and the Stock Exchanges: Historical Resources by Science, Technology and Business Division 

 Published/Created: 2019 

 The selection of resources included in this guide are intended for those researching the history of Wall Street and includes resources for those interested in researching the history of the various American stock exchanges. 

## Internet Resources 

The links below are for content on the Library of Congress website or more generally on the internet.

- Bank Failures and the FDIC, March 23, 2023 (Congressional Research Service) (PDF, 575KB) This link opens in a new window 

 This In Focus report provides an introduction to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s (FDIC’s) process for resolving failing FDIC-insured banks. It also identifies policy issues Congress may consider related to the recent failures of two large banks in 2023—Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) and Signature Bank. 
- Banking Act of 1933 - Glass-Steagall Act (FRASER, Federal Reserve) External This link opens in a new window 

 This link provides a downloadable version of the text of the Banking Act of 1933. 
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) This link opens in a new window 

 The CFPB is a U.S. government agency dedicated to making sure you are treated fairly by banks, lenders and other financial institutions. It provides consumer education, data & research, and takes consumer complaints. 
- Data.gov This link opens in a new window 

 This search on the data.gov search defaults to data and datasets from the FDIC, including information on historical financial information and failed banks. 
- Deposit Insurance and the Failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, March 27, 2023 (Congressional Research Service) (PDF, 568 KB) This link opens in a new window 

 This In Focus report examines the role of deposit insurance in the financial system and addresses policy considerations for the 118th Congress in the wake of recent turmoil in the banking system precipitated by the failures of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) and Signature Bank. 
- Dodd–Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, PUBLIC LAW 111–203—JULY 21, 2010 (PDF, 2.2 MB) This link opens in a new window 

 To promote the financial stability of the United States by improving accountability and transparency in the financial system, to end ‘‘too big to fail’’, to protect the American taxpayer by ending bailouts, to protect consumers from abusive financial services practices, and for other purposes. 
- FDIC Archive This link opens in a new window 

 The Archive includes press releases, annual reports, FDIC Consumer News, speeches & testimony, research publications, lists of banks examined, active financial institution letters, Federal Register Notices, and more.
